recentItems.title: Vlad Reacts to Lil Durk Being Found Not Guilty on All Charges
recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join
--------
VladTV’s Vlad the Butcher responds to Lil Durk’s not guilty verdict, breaking down why the jury may have found reasonable doubt in the murder-for-hire case tied to Quando Rondo and the death of Lil Pop. Vlad discusses the prosecution’s evidence, including witnesses, text messages, phone records, alleged payments, and why he believes there was “no smoking gun” directly linking Durk to an order.

He also examines the role of Durk’s defense team, including Drew Findling and Brian Steele, and questions the credibility of cooperating witnesses such as OTF Jam and OTF Vonnie, who were facing serious prison time. The segment also touches on King Von, Lil Tim, Trap Lore Ross, possible civil litigation, and the emotional fallout for everyone involved.

A measured reaction to a closely watched hip-hop legal case, with condolences to Lil Pop’s family and perspective on the cost of street conflicts.

--------
Attorney Mohammed Gangat joins VladTV to break down major developments in several high-profile hip-hop criminal cases, including the Lil Durk murder-for-hire trial, Keefe D's conviction, Tory Lanez, and the legal situation surrounding Pooh Shiesty.
Gangat analyzes testimony from Vani K. Von Grant, who admitted involvement in multiple violent incidents while describing his relationship with Lil Durk and members of his circle. Prosecutors are using Grant's proximity to Durk—including allegedly working as his assistant and staying at his home—to help establish connections within the alleged murder-for-hire conspiracy. Mohammed and Vlad also examine the government's use of music videos, lyrics, podcasts, clothing, and other evidence to connect defendants to the case.
The conversation then turns to Keefe D, whose jury returned a guilty verdict after approximately 90 minutes of deliberation. Gangat explains how prosecutors can build a successful case using circumstantial evidence and compares the strategy to other major trials.
They also revisit Tory Lanez's conviction, analyzing how prosecutor questioning affected crucial eyewitness testimony, before discussing the complicated legal situation involving Pooh Shiesty and whether witnesses such as Gucci Mane could ultimately testify.
Finally, Mohammed and Vlad debate one of the biggest decisions facing defendants in serious criminal trials: whether to testify in their own defense. With defendants potentially facing life without parole, Gangat explains the enormous risks of taking the stand and allowing prosecutors to cross-examine them.

--------

Former Army Ranger and sniper Nicholas Irving joins Shawn Prez to weigh in on the disputed accounts surrounding the Osama bin Laden raid and the public clash between Rob O’Neill and Matt Bissonnette. Irving, who says he knows both former SEAL Team Six operators, discusses O’Neill’s VladTV interview, Bissonnette’s book *No Easy Day*, conflicting after-action memories, and the “fog of war” inside the Abbottabad compound. He also addresses claims about a possible unnamed operator known as “Red,” the role of money, history, and reputation, plus O’Neill’s reported $25 million lawsuit against podcast hosts calling him a fraud. Drawing from his own combat experience, Irving explains why multiple team members may have fired rounds and why special operations secrets often stay inside the fraternity. The conversation also touches on veteran-on-veteran conflict, Hollywood’s *SEAL Team*, and the lasting legacy of who killed Bin Laden.

Judge Greg Mathis returns to VladTV for an uncensored legal breakdown of major hip-hop and true-crime cases. He weighs the evidence in Keefe D’s Nevada trial over Tupac Shakur’s 1996 Las Vegas killing, discussing reasonable doubt, the Mike Tyson fight, Death Row rumors, and why a hung jury or plea deal could be possible. Mathis also analyzes Lil Durk’s federal case, OTF ties, Quando Rondo, King Von, OTM Jam’s cooperation, OTF Vonnie’s testimony, and what prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt.

The conversation expands to Diddy and Cassie, Big U, street politics, off-duty security, and the use of rap lyrics in RICO-style cases. Mathis also reacts to Daejon Love’s alleged romance-investment scam, D4vd’s legal situation and public defender reports, plus broader debates on murder trials, mental illness, John Hinckley Jr., Lindsey Clancy, and the death penalty.

Part 1: https://youtu.be/K7__iCx2ghE
--------
Attorney Bradford Cohen sits down with Vlad to address his brief role on Pooh Shiesty’s federal kidnapping and robbery case, explaining why he stepped away after about a month without revealing confidential details. Cohen pushes back on internet rumors that he left because the case was “bad,” saying he routinely takes difficult criminal cases and wasn’t afraid of the evidence. He discusses the Dallas/Texas bond hearing, the FBI’s early presentation, missing guns, the alleged contract issue, and later developments including the leaked Gucci Mane video and FedEx Kinko’s records. Cohen also speaks on federal court strategy, possible defenses, and why cases can change as witnesses and evidence develop. He praises Pooh Shiesty, says there is no animosity, and notes he recommended respected attorneys, including Brian Steele, to help the rapper’s defense. Watch for insight into hip-hop legal battles, criminal defense tactics, and high-profile federal cases.

--------
Chingy joins VladTV for a candid conversation about the music business, bad record deals, and why artists need lawyers, negotiation skills, and trusted people around them before signing contracts. Reflecting on his own career lessons, the St. Louis rapper explains that business disputes should be handled through renegotiation—not violence or intimidation—and warns young artists about “sharks” and “vultures” chasing money in the industry.

The discussion turns to character, integrity, and trust as Vlad and Chingy compare contracts, handshake deals, relationships, and reputation. Chingy pushes back on the idea that good people are destined to lose, arguing that integrity can take you far unless unethical people actively work to keep others down. He also emphasizes spiritual currency, professionalism, being on time, and treating people with respect as keys to long-term success in hip-hop and entertainment.

Part 1: https://youtu.be/FoBBj-6j544
--------
In this VladTV interview, Max B revisits his Dipset-era run with Jim Jones, Cam’ron and ByrdGang, offering new context on the long-running debate around “We Fly High (Ballin’).” The Harlem rapper clarifies that he wrote the chorus—not the full record—and says Jim Jones wrote his verses, while also explaining why he no longer wants credit for the hit. Max B reflects on appearing in the California-shot music video, the song reaching No. 5 on Billboard, and how their studio chemistry shaped hundreds of records.

He also looks back on projects like M.O.B., work with Stack Bundles, “Life in the Fast Lane,” “American Gangster,” and his role on Cam’ron’s “You Gotta Love It,” a Jay-Z diss he says he approached from a neutral stance. The conversation highlights Max B’s influence, versatility, and creative impact during a pivotal era in New York hip-hop.

recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join

Part 1: https://youtu.be/-pWadYhoSkc
--------
In this VladTV segment, Mario Sanchez revisits 1997 at New Folsom’s C Yard, where he says he became the Norteño shot caller “by default” after others were removed from the yard. Speaking with Vlad, Sanchez explains how 40 to 50 Norteños operated under his direction, from daily yard security protocols to the politics of holding territory inside prison. He details what it meant to “have a yard,” the role of numbers against South Siders, and how internal informants and a conflict with white inmates pushed him toward leaving that life behind. Sanchez also clarifies that he was never part of a prison gang like NF, saying he has been inactive since 1997. Now living in Los Angeles, he discusses moving differently, staying out of trouble, and handling business after prison.
